title: The Spindle Tells the Cell Where to Cut

scenes.tts: An animal cell has sorted its chromosomes into two sets. Now it must cut itself in two. But where? The furrow, the inward fold that does the cutting, forms midway between the two sets. That position is not an accident. The spindle, the array of microtubules that pulled the chromosomes apart, sends the signal.
scenes.visual: A round cell with two chromosome sets; three question-mark cut lines; the middle one becomes a furrow mark; the spindle appears and sends a signal to the cortex at the midpoint.
scenes.narration: An animal cell has sorted its chromosomes into two sets. Now it must cut itself in two. But where? The furrow, the inward fold that does the cutting, forms midway between the two sets. That position is not an accident. The spindle, the array of microtubules that pulled the chromosomes apart, sends the signal.

scenes.tts: The signal is a small switch protein called RhoA. It is on when it holds G T P, and off when it holds G D P. At the equator, an enzyme called Ect2 switches it on. Ect2 swaps G D P for G T P. Researchers then made active RhoA visible. They fused a green fluorescent protein to a fragment that binds only G T P bound RhoA. The glow marks where RhoA is on, not where the protein simply sits.
scenes.caption: The signal is a small switch protein called RhoA. It is on when it holds GTP, and off when it holds GDP. At the equator, an enzyme called Ect2 switches it on. Ect2 swaps GDP for GTP. Researchers then made active RhoA visible. They fused a green fluorescent protein to a fragment that binds only GTP-bound RhoA. The glow marks where RhoA is on, not where the protein simply sits.
scenes.visual: RhoA chip grey with GDP; Ect2 swaps GDP for GTP and RhoA turns green; a probe docks only on the GTP form and glows; a green band lights on the cell equator.
scenes.narration: The signal is a small switch protein called RhoA. It is on when it holds GTP, and off when it holds GDP. At the equator, an enzyme called Ect2 switches it on. Ect2 swaps GDP for GTP. Researchers then made active RhoA visible. They fused a green fluorescent protein to a fragment that binds only GTP-bound RhoA. The glow marks where RhoA is on, not where the protein simply sits.

scenes.tts: Active RhoA gathers in a bounded band at the equator. The band appears one to four minutes before the furrow. This was seen in sea urchin embryos and in frog embryos. Next, the researchers blocked actin assembly with drugs. In sea urchin embryos, the band still formed. So RhoA switches on before the actin ring, and does not need it.
scenes.visual: Timeline: green band then, one to four minutes later, the furrow. Then a drug blocks the actin step; the band still forms; RhoA zone then actin ring order is shown.
scenes.narration: Active RhoA gathers in a bounded band at the equator. The band appears one to four minutes before the furrow. This was seen in sea urchin embryos and in frog embryos. Next, the researchers blocked actin assembly with drugs. In sea urchin embryos, the band still formed. So RhoA switches on before the actin ring, and does not need it.

scenes.tts: In sea urchin cells already furrowing, the researchers pushed the spindle aside with a blunt needle. The band relocated over three to five minutes, and the furrow followed it. Move the spindle, and the signal moves first. The delay argues against the spindle simply dragging the cortex along.
scenes.visual: A needle pushes the spindle sideways; the green band slides to the spindle's new midpoint over three to five minutes; the furrow follows; a row of three chips lights in order: spindle, band, furrow.
scenes.narration: In sea urchin cells already furrowing, the researchers pushed the spindle aside with a blunt needle. The band relocated over three to five minutes, and the furrow followed it. scenes.tts: Active RhoA turns on formins, which build long actin filaments. It also promotes myosin II, a motor that pulls actin filaments past each other. Together they make a contractile ring under the membrane, and as it tightens, the furrow ingresses. Ingression leaves a thin bridge between the daughters. Later, in several animal cell systems, E S C R T three assembles in the bridge, constricts it and cuts it.
scenes.caption: Active RhoA turns on formins, which build long actin filaments. It also promotes myosin II, a motor that pulls actin filaments past each other. Together they make a contractile ring under the membrane, and as it tightens, the furrow ingresses. Ingression leaves a thin bridge between the daughters. Later, in several animal cell systems, ESCRT-III assembles in the bridge, constricts it and cuts it.
scenes.visual: RhoA turns on formin, which grows bead filaments; myosin slides two filaments past each other; the ring forms at the band, the furrow deepens to a thin bridge between two daughters; ESCRT-III rings narrow the bridge until it is cut.
scenes.narration: Active RhoA turns on formins, which build long actin filaments. It also promotes myosin II, a motor that pulls actin filaments past each other. Together they make a contractile ring under the membrane, and as it tightens, the furrow ingresses. Ingression leaves a thin bridge between the daughters. Later, in several animal cell systems, ESCRT-III assembles in the bridge, constricts it and cuts it.

scenes.tts: These timings come from large embryonic cells, so do not assume the same minutes in a human cell. The drawstring ring is a standard cartoon, and filament arrangement differs between systems. Keep the rule: the spindle places the signal, and the furrow follows the signal.
scenes.visual: A box of embryonic-cell timings beside a dashed question box for a human cell; the ring drawing rearranges to show arrangements differ; then the chain spindle, band, furrow.
